segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: For many English learners, speaking is the most difficult part of the language to master.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: To improve your speaking skills, you need to be able to practice with other English learners or English speakers.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: One way to do this is by joining – or starting – an English club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In today’s Education Tips, we discuss how English clubs can be helpful to your language-learning process.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This is part one of a two-part series on English clubs.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In this episode, we offer advice for how to start and organize an English club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In next week’s episode, we will suggest some fun and educational activities for your club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: There are many reasons why English clubs can help learners of all ages and levels improve their English.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The most important reason is that they offer learners a chance to practice English by actually speaking it.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: There are other advantages, too.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: English clubs are less formal than a classroom setting.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Many learners find them more fun than usual English classes.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: They also let learners practice English in more real-life situations.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This can increase a learner’s desire to practice and learn on their own.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Bonnie Norton and Ernst Von Glasersfeld are learning theory experts.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: They say that using a language in authentic situations is very important for learners.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: So is being motivated to practice and improve, they say.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Now that you understand some of the benefits of an English club, let’s discus how you can create your own club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The first step in starting an English club is to find club members.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: There are different ways to do this.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If you are a teacher creating the club for your students, then the easiest way is to put up signs in classrooms advertising the club’s first meeting.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You can also pass around a sign-up sheet in classes.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If you are trying to start a club at your place of work, you can advertise your club by sending an email around to coworkers.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You can also put up signs about the club around the workplace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If your club is open for anyone to join, you can use the internet to find members.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Websites such as Meetup or Facebook are great places to announce club meetings and communicate with members.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Next, you must find a place for your club to meet.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This step is very important.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The location of your club will affect how many people come to your meetings.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It is important to consider several things when choosing a location.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: First, how easy is it for members to find and get to the location?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It is a good idea to find a central location that is easy to get to.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Otherwise, members may slowly stop coming.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Second, it is important to find a location that is safe.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You want your members to feel comfortable as they are arriving and leaving.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If you are a teacher, the easiest location is probably in a classroom or another room in the school building.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: English clubs often meet after school or work hours.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This can make it easier to find an available room.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If you are creating an English club outside of a class or work setting, consider holding meetings at a cafe, restaurant or bar.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: These places often have enough space for large groups.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Club members coming straight from school or work will also have a chance to eat or drink something.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Wherever you meet, make sure to speak with the owners of the business or building and get their permission.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The third step is to hold your first meeting.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The first meeting is important for every English club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It is a good idea to use the first meeting as a chance to talk with members about logistics.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This includes how often and where the club will meet, whether or not there will be membership fees, and how the club leadership will work.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Club leadership is one of the most important parts of starting an English club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If you have a good system of leadership, your club has a better chance at lasting.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If your club is small enough, or more informal, sometimes all you need is one person to lead the club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The main responsibility of the one leader is to organize and lead the meetings.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The leader also must communicate information to club members.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: However, if your club is large, it is a good idea to have a group of people that can help run the club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This kind of leadership is useful for many reasons.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It divides the amount of work it takes to run a club among several people.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It also helps club members practice speaking English with real-life tasks.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: And, if the members of your club are mostly students, it can help them develop teamwork and leadership skills.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It is also important to have rules for the leadership system.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: For example, how long will club leaders hold their positions?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: How will they transfer power to someone else if they must quit the club?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You should consider holding elections to choose new leaders.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Whatever leadership system you choose, the goal of an English club remains the same: to keep your club members motivated to continue participating.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: So, club leaders should not try to do everything themselves.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In fact, it is a good idea to give tasks to many different club members.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: This makes the members feel important.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: They are more likely to remain committed to the club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: And it can increase their desire to learn.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: English clubs can take many forms and serve many purposes.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Following these steps will help any club have a successful start.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Join us next week as we talk about fun and creative activities to do with your newly formed English club.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Sherlock Holmes is an imaginary private detective created by British writer Arthur Conan Doyle in the late 1880s.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Doyle’s stories about the detective have been turned into movies and television shows.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: One of Sherlock Holmes’ great skills is a powerful memory.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In a recent BBC television series, the character uses a memory technique called a “mind palace” or “memory palace.”

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: On one show, for example, Holmes has been severely wounded in a shooting and retreats into his mind to search for ways to survive.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: He visits rooms in his mind palace, looking for helpful memories.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In one room, he finds his childhood dog, and the memory helps calm the detective.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The memory palace idea was not a BBC creation.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The method for remembering has existed for thousands of years.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Many language educators today teach their students how to use the method to improve their language skills.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: But what exactly is a memory palace?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It is a real structure, such as a home or building, that you can picture in your head.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You then imagine placing things you want to remember inside the structure.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You can use a memory palace to remember words, phrases, facts, or even the order of events.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If you can see the inside of a house or building in your mind, you can make your own memory palace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: On today’s Education Tips, we will show you how.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Start with a list of words or phrases that you want to remember.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Then, close your eyes and choose a physical space that you know well, such as your home, a school you attended, or a current or former workplace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: If your chosen space has only one or two rooms, do not worry.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You can also use things like doors, passageways, steps or other permanent places along the physical path.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The next step is to imagine walking through the space using the path that you would normally take through it.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: As you walk through, put objects that you want to remember at specific places along the path.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Leave the objects there to pick up later when you visit your memory palace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Now, let’s try this technique by using six ingredients for a pizza: flour, water, dry yeast, tomato sauce, cheese and basil.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Close your eyes and picture a home.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: First, you open the front door and see a bag of flour on the floor.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The bag is broken and some of the flour has spilled.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You are worried that you might slip, so you carefully step over the area.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Second, you walk into your bedroom.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: On top of your bed sits a cup of water.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The cup is shaped like an upside-down piece of pizza.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You think about how funny that is and laugh about it.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Third, as you enter the living room, you see a very large spoon of dry yeast sitting on the sofa.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The spoon is watching a cooking show on television.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Fourth, while standing in the living room, you notice the room has a strange smell to it.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You look above the television and see a block of cheese hanging on the wall.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Fifth, you walk into the kitchen and see two tomatoes chasing each other around the room.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Suddenly, they crash and explode, covering the floor in red.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: And sixth, you open the back door and go outside.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: There, you see a group of very tall green basil plants.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In a funny voice, the tallest plant says, “Choose me!

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Choose me!”

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Did you notice anything strange about the palace?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: It was full of extraordinary and humorous imagery.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: We will say more about that in a few minutes.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: But first, let’s check how well our technique worked.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: See if you can answer these questions:

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: 1-What was on the wall above the television?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: 2-Where were the tomatoes and what were they doing?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: 3-Which object was sitting on the bed?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: 4-Where was the yeast and what was it doing?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: 5-Which ingredient spoke and what did it say?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: 6-What did you see when you opened the front door?

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: My guess is that you remembered everything in our memory palace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: That’s good news.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Experts offer some advice for making strong memory palaces.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: For instance, if you want to remember a lot of words, memory trainer Anthony Metivier suggests first drawing a simple map of your memory palace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Then, number the places along your path where you will put the things that you want to remember.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: You can put more than one thing in each room or area.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Later, you will add the mental imagery.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: English teacher James, of the YouTube channel JamesESL English Lessons, has additional advice.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: In his video on memory palaces, he says that there are three keys to a strong memory palace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: They are: emotion, movement, and connections between the object and something permanent.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Both he and Metivier say imagining things in a humorous or crazy way improves your ability to remember them.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: These experts also agree that connecting images to actions or movement will create lasting memories.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: For instance, the tomatoes were chasing each other and the basil spoke.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: And finally, teacher James suggests placing the objects next to or on something permanent in your palace.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Beds, sofas, floors, walls, doors – all of these are permanent.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: The block of cheese was on the wall, for example.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Now, it’s your turn.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Pick a list of English words or phrases that you have trouble remembering and try this method on your own.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Let us know how it goes.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: I’m John Russell.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: And I’m Alice Bryant.
